title: The Social Contract
hook: Why should anyone obey the state? The social contract answers: people trade some freedom for the security and order that only collective authority can provide.
key_points: The social contract is the idea that political authority rests on an implicit agreement among the people.
Individuals give up some unlimited freedom in exchange for protection, order, and shared rules.
Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau gave rival versions — from a strong sovereign to government by consent.
It grounds the modern claim that legitimate power flows from the governed, not from force or birth.
content_html: The social contract is a way of answering one of politics' oldest questions: what makes the state's authority legitimate, and why should anyone obey it? The answer it offers is an agreement. Imagine life with no shared authority at all — no one to enforce promises or punish harm. To escape that insecurity, the theory says, people implicitly agree to accept common rules and a power that enforces them, trading away some of their unlimited freedom for the order and protection that only collective authority can provide.
extra_html: The idea took its modern shape with three thinkers who disagreed sharply about the terms. Thomas Hobbes, writing amid civil war, argued that the danger of life without order was so great that people should submit to a strong, near-absolute sovereign. John Locke countered that the contract is conditional: government exists to protect natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and forfeits its authority if it betrays that trust — a line of thought that fed directly into later revolutions. Jean-Jacques Rousseau reframed it around the "general will," the shared interest of the community as a whole. As Encyclopaedia Britannica notes, these are competing models rather than one fixed doctrine, but together they established the enduring modern claim that legitimate power flows from the consent of the governed rather than from force, conquest, or birth.

related.title: What Government Is For
related.hook: Every society needs a way to make and enforce collective decisions — that shared system of authority is what we call government.

related.title: Political Legitimacy
related.hook: Power can rest on fear alone, but it lasts when people believe it is rightful. That belief — legitimacy — is what separates authority from mere force.

related.title: What Democracy Means
related.hook: Rule by the people: a system where political power ultimately traces back to citizens, usually through regular, free elections.

related.title: The Enlightenment & Modern Politics
related.hook: The radical idea that legitimate power comes from the people — not God or birth — was forged in the Enlightenment, and it still underpins democracy today.

flashcards.prompt: In one line, what is the social contract?
flashcards.back_html: The idea that political authority rests on an implicit agreement: people accept shared rules and authority in exchange for order and protection they couldn't secure alone.

flashcards.prompt: What do people give up under the social contract, and what do they get?

choices.text: Some unlimited freedom, in exchange for security and shared rules
All their property, in exchange for a guaranteed income
Their right to vote, in exchange for lower taxes

flashcards.explanation_html: The core trade is a measure of unrestrained liberty for the order and protection that collective authority makes possible.

flashcards.prompt: Which thinkers are most associated with rival versions of the social contract?
flashcards.explanation_html: Hobbes argued for a strong sovereign, Locke for government by consent and natural rights, and Rousseau for the collective "general will."
